Vesta. The second-most-massive body in the asteroid belt and a prototype of the differentiated asteroid — a small planetary body with an iron core, rocky mantle, and basaltic crust. Named for the Roman goddess of the hearth, it is one of the few asteroids visible to the naked eye under dark skies. The Dawn spacecraft's study of Vesta revealed it to be geologically complex, bearing the scars of a massive ancient impact and evidence of volcanic activity dating to the early solar system.

Vesta was discovered on March 29th, 1807 by Heinrich Olbers, and named for Vesta, goddess of the hearth and home. It is one of the few naked-eye asteroids. The asteroid is the second-largest in its belt, with a diameter of roughly 525 kilometers. Only Ceres is more massive in the belt, but Vesta is far denser and internally differentiated with a core-mantle-crust structure.

Its surface is basaltic, composed of howardite rock and other igneous materials. The spectral reflectance matches eucrite meteorites found on Earth, establishing Vesta as a parent body for meteorite families. The asteroid has a massive south-pole impact crater called the Rheasilvia basin, roughly 500 kilometers across, excavated about a billion years ago. The collision ejected thousands of fragments into heliocentric orbits, forming the Vesta family.

Seismic data and density models indicate a metallic core, revealing that Vesta melted and separated into layers early in solar-system history, within roughly five million years of formation. Its high albedo, or reflectivity, makes it visible without optical aid. Ancient heating from short-lived isotopes like aluminum-26 powered the volcanism and differentiation.

Vesta and Ceres together dominate the asteroid belt's mass, representing opposite extremes — differentiated rock versus icy dwarf. Vesta is the signature example of a main-belt asteroid and the source of common meteorite types in museum collections, and the Rheasilvia event exemplifies bombardment in the early solar system and its role in planetary formation.
